intro:
The exercises in this chapter all push toward one habit: derive the synchronization primitive from the access pattern, not from instinct or from the primitive you reached for in C++ or Go. A short contended mutation wants a Mutex; a read-mostly snapshot wants an RwLock; a single-word flag or counter wants an atomic; a thread that must wait on a predicate wants a Condvar paired with that predicate's mutex; a phase boundary wants a Barrier; and a subsystem with one logical owner usually wants a channel instead of any shared lock at all. The warm-up and design exercises train the classification step, while the implementation and debugging exercises make you confront the two failure modes that actually ship: misordered locks and condvar waits that trust wakeup instead of re-checking state.

The through-line is that in Rust the lock owns the data. A Mutex<T> hands out a guard, and the guard is a borrow whose lifetime is the critical section; the atomic publication pattern is the same idea expressed without a lock, where a Release store and an Acquire load form the happens-before edge that lets a reader trust everything the writer did beforehand. Keep that ownership-and-visibility framing in view and every exercise below reduces to the same question: who owns this mutation, and who needs to see it.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose Mutex, RwLock, Condvar, atomic, barrier, or channel from the workload
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Work through the six cases by asking the decision-order questions in turn: is the state shared and mutable at all, are readers frequent, is waiting involved, and does the invariant fit in one machine word.

The shared mutable retry map is the only case that is genuinely shared mutable state with no read/write skew worth exploiting: many workers both read and modify it constantly. That is a Mutex<HashMap<...>>. A retry table is mutated on essentially every access, so the read-write distinction buys nothing and a plain mutex is the calmest fit.

The read-mostly config snapshot is a read-mostly state boundary. Every request reads it and only an occasional reload writes it, so an RwLock<Config> lets the many readers proceed in parallel and the rare writer take exclusivity. Even better, if the config is replaced wholesale rather than mutated field by field, an Arc<Config> swapped atomically removes the lock entirely.

The worker waiting for a non-empty queue is a waited-on predicate under one mutex: the predicate is queue.is_empty(), it lives under a Mutex, and the worker uses a Condvar to sleep until it might have changed. The condvar is not the source of truth; the mutex-protected predicate is, which is why the wait belongs in a loop (see Exercise 5).

The hot metrics counter is small enough for atomics: a single AtomicU64 incremented with fetch_add carries the whole invariant in one word, so no lock is needed. The startup start-gun for several workers is a phase boundary, not a state container: a Barrier::new(n) releases all workers at once and holds no data of its own. Finally, the single owner thread receiving commands wants ownership transfer rather than shared mutation: an mpsc channel hands owned commands to the one owner, so there is no shared lock to reason about at all.

The distinction the exercise asks you to keep sharp is condvar-predicate versus channel-handoff. A condvar coordinates threads around state that several of them touch under a shared mutex; a channel moves owned values to a single owner so the state stops being shared. If the queue should belong to exactly one thread, the channel is simpler; if multiple threads must inspect and mutate the same protected queue, the condvar design is the honest one. Atomics are deliberately last on the list for the counter only, because treating atomics as the default answer for every shared-state problem leads straight to memory-ordering bugs that a mutex or channel would have avoided.
criteria: Each of the six cases is mapped to a primitive (Mutex, RwLock, Condvar, atomic, Barrier, channel) and justified by the shape of its state and access pattern.
The condvar-predicate case (waiting on queue.is_empty() under a mutex) is contrasted explicitly with the channel-handoff case (owned commands to one owner).
Atomics are reserved for the single-word counter and explicitly rejected as a default for the map, the config, and the queue.

exerciseSolutions.title: Replace a Mutex with RwLock where appropriate
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Start from the access pattern, not the type. With Arc<Mutex<HashMap<String, Config>>>, every lookup of a route's config calls lock() and serializes against every other lookup, even though lookups never conflict with each other. Reads dominate and writes happen only on occasional reloads, so the lock is serializing operations that are logically read-only.

Under an RwLock<HashMap<String, Config>>, every config lookup becomes config.read(), and only the reload path becomes config.write(). The workload assumption that makes this plausible is exactly the stated one: reads vastly outnumber writes, and a read holds the lock only long enough to clone or copy out the value it needs. Many readers can then hold the lock concurrently, so on a multi-core server the read path stops being a single-lane bottleneck.

An RwLock is not automatically the better choice, and naming a case where it is the wrong upgrade is required. If writes were frequent, the writer would repeatedly have to wait for all readers to drain and then exclude everyone, which can starve and is often slower than a mutex's simple alternation; depending on the implementation, frequent writers can also starve under reader-preferring policies. And if each critical section is tiny, for example a single HashMap lookup that copies out one small Config, the extra bookkeeping an RwLock does to track reader counts can cost more than the contention it removes. In both of those cases a plain Mutex stays calmer and frequently faster. The signal for RwLock is read-mostly access with non-trivial read sections, not a desire to make the code look more concurrent.

Finally, distinguish the primitive change from the ownership-model change. Swapping Mutex for RwLock is a local tactical edit; it keeps the same shared-mutable design. The larger change is to stop sharing mutable state at all. If reloads replace the whole table, store an Arc<HashMap<String, Config>> (or Arc<Config> per route) and publish a new immutable snapshot on reload while readers keep their old Arc until they drop it; readers then take no lock and never block each other or the writer. Alternatively, give the config one owner thread and have it answer requests over a channel. Those are not 'a faster lock'; they remove the lock by changing who owns mutation.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: RwLock as a read-mostly tactical fit, with an immutable-snapshot alternative that removes the lock by changing ownership.
criteria: The lookup path maps to read() and the reload path to write(), and read-mostly access is named as the main signal for considering RwLock.
At least one wrong-upgrade case is given: frequent writes (writer starvation) or tiny read sections where RwLock bookkeeping outweighs a Mutex.
The local Mutex-to-RwLock swap is distinguished from the larger ownership change of immutable Arc snapshots or a one-owner channel.

exerciseSolutions.title: Reason about Acquire and Release in a toy publication protocol
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The protocol publishes one payload word through one flag. The writer stores the payload, then stores true into the flag; the reader loads the flag and, only if it is true, loads the payload. The whole correctness argument rests on which atomic operation carries the ordering edge.

Keep the payload word relaxed. A Relaxed store and Relaxed load are still atomic, so the reader never sees a torn value, but Relaxed imposes no ordering on the surrounding memory operations. That is fine here because the payload does not need to order anything on its own; it is the thing being published, not the thing doing the publishing.

Put the ordering on the flag. The writer uses Ordering::Release on the flag store. A Release store guarantees that every write the writer performed before it, in particular the payload store, is visible to any thread that later performs an Acquire load which observes that store. The reader uses Ordering::Acquire on the flag load. When the Acquire load reads true, it establishes a happens-before edge with the writer's Release store, and therefore the reader is guaranteed to also see the payload write that preceded it. This is the canonical release/acquire publication pair.

The key insight the exercise wants you to articulate is why the flag, not the payload load, carries the ordering edge. The flag is the single point both threads agree to synchronize on: the writer's last action and the reader's first decision. The release/acquire relationship is a property of that one pair of operations on the same atomic. The payload load can stay relaxed precisely because the Acquire load of the flag has already fenced everything that happened before the matching Release store. If the consumer has not performed an Acquire load that observed the flag as true, it has no right to trust the payload; loading the payload first, or loading the flag with Relaxed, would break the publication and could legally read a stale zero on a weakly ordered machine. This is exactly the design the runnable lab implements, and it prints ready = true and value = 42.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Release/Acquire publication: the flag carries the happens-before edge, the payload stays relaxed.
criteria: The writer publishes the flag with Ordering::Release.
The consumer loads the flag with Ordering::Acquire before it trusts the published state.
The payload word stays Relaxed and the runnable lab prints ready = true and value = 42.
The explanation states that the flag, not the payload load, carries the ordering edge because release/acquire synchronizes the one shared atomic both threads agree on.

exerciseSolutions.title: Find and fix a deadlock scenario
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is a lock-order inversion that creates a circular wait. Thread A acquires accounts and then tries to acquire audit; Thread B acquires audit and then tries to acquire accounts. The deadlock condition is the moment both threads have taken their first lock and are each blocked waiting on the lock the other holds: A holds accounts and waits for audit, B holds audit and waits for accounts. Neither will release until it makes progress, and neither can make progress, so both wait forever. That this is rare is irrelevant; it is a structural property of the code, not a statistical fluke, and it will eventually be hit in production. All four Coffman conditions hold, but the only one under our control here is the circular wait, so that is the one we break.

The mechanically enforceable repair is a single global lock order that every path obeys: always lock accounts before audit, never the reverse. Once both threads acquire in the same order, the cycle is impossible, because no thread can hold the later lock while requesting the earlier one. This is enforceable rather than a plea to 'be careful' if you funnel both subsystems through one helper that takes the locks in the fixed order, so no call site can get it wrong. The fix is to impose one global ordering that both threads obey.

Lock ordering is the minimal repair, but it is not always the best one, and the exercise asks you to justify the choice. Two stronger options reshape the problem so the second lock disappears. First, make one subsystem the owner: if audit is really a log, give it a single owner thread and send audit records over a channel, so the account path never locks audit at all and there is no second lock to order. Second, reconsider whether the two locks need to be held together. If the only reason both are locked is to keep an account update and its audit entry atomic, you can record the audit event after releasing the accounts lock (accepting a brief window where the update is visible before its audit line), or consolidate the truly-coupled state under one lock so a single critical section covers both. The decision rule: if the two pieces of state are genuinely independent and only incidentally touched together, lock ordering or a channel owner is the clean fix; if they form one invariant, consolidate them under one lock so there is no second lock to invert.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Global lock ordering: both paths acquire accounts before audit through one helper, breaking the circular wait.
criteria: The circular-wait condition is stated concretely: A holds accounts and waits for audit while B holds audit and waits for accounts.
The proposed repair (one global lock order enforced through a single helper) is mechanically enforceable, not advisory.
The answer weighs lock ordering against state reshaping (consolidating the coupled state) and ownership transfer (a channel-owned audit log) and gives a rule for choosing among them.

exerciseSolutions.title: Repair a condvar wait loop before it flakes under load
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is wakeup-as-truth. The worker does if queue.is_empty() { condvar.wait(...) } and then assumes a job is ready as soon as it wakes. An if is the wrong shape because a condvar wakeup does not promise the predicate is now true; it only tells the waiter to re-check. Three things can wake a single if-guarded wait and leave the queue empty: a spurious wakeup (permitted by the platform and the API), a notify_all that wakes several waiters when only one job arrived so all but one find the queue empty again, and a wakeup that races against another consumer that already drained the queue. After any of those, the worker proceeds to pop from an empty queue and panics or misbehaves. Under load these races become frequent rather than theoretical.

The fix is to re-check the predicate in a loop. Replace the if with a while that re-evaluates the predicate every time wait returns, and only leave the loop when the predicate genuinely holds. The predicate that belongs under the mutex is the shared queue state itself, queue.is_empty() (and, in a closeable queue, the closed flag), because that is the real source of truth. The condvar only wakes the worker; the queue state under the mutex remains the real predicate. This is exactly the structure of the chapter's mutex-plus-condvar example, where the worker holds the lock and loops on while state.jobs.is_empty() && !state.closed, calling wait inside the loop so it re-checks after every wakeup.

The notifier side matters too. The notifying thread must update the predicate, in this design push a job or set closed, while it holds the same mutex, and only then call notify. If it notified before updating the state, a waiter could wake, re-check, find nothing, and sleep again, losing the signal. Updating the mutex-protected state first and notifying after guarantees that any waiter that re-acquires the lock observes the change. The mutex-protected state and the condvar are one design, not two independent pieces.

Finally, note when a channel is simpler. If exactly one thread should own and drain the queue, an mpsc channel removes the shared queue, the mutex, and the condvar all at once: producers send owned jobs, and the single consumer's recv blocks until an item arrives and returns it directly, with no predicate to re-check and no spurious-wakeup handling. The condvar design is correct and is the right tool when several threads must coordinate around the same protected queue, but a one-owner channel is the simpler design when the queue has a single natural owner.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Predicate-in-a-loop: wait re-checks the mutex-protected queue after each wakeup; the producer updates state before notifying.
criteria: The if is replaced with a while loop that re-checks the predicate after each wakeup, replacing wakeup-as-truth with predicate-in-a-loop reasoning.
The shared queue state under the mutex is named as the source of truth that remains authoritative after wakeup, with the notifier updating it before calling notify.
At least one case is given where a one-owner mpsc channel removes the shared queue, mutex, and condvar entirely.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose the right primitive for a service under load
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Walk the pipeline accept -> parse -> route -> update metrics -> consult config -> enqueue work -> wait for completion -> publish result and assign each stage the primitive its access pattern demands, keeping each mutable subsystem with one obvious owner wherever possible.

Immutable shared state with Arc only: the routing table and the parsed request. The routing rules are read on every request and rarely change, so publish them as an Arc<RoutingTable> and swap the Arc on reload; readers clone the Arc and take no lock. The parsed request is owned by the request's own task and never shared mutably, so it needs no synchronization at all.

Mutex or RwLock: the config snapshot is the candidate for RwLock, and only because it is genuinely read-mostly, consulted on every request and rewritten only on occasional reloads, which is the read-mostly pattern that justifies the choice rather than aesthetics. If the config is replaced wholesale rather than edited in place, prefer the immutable Arc<Config> swap and drop the lock entirely. A Mutex is appropriate only for small contended mutable state that is genuinely shared and write-heavy, for example an in-flight or retry table that workers mutate on nearly every access; there the read/write split buys nothing.

Owned commands and results over channels: enqueue work and wait for completion. Submit owned work items to a worker pool over an mpsc (or bounded sync_channel) so the queue has a single owner and there is no shared lock; the bounded variant also gives backpressure. Wait for completion with a per-request oneshot-style channel: the worker sends the owned result back and the request thread blocks on recv until it arrives. Then publish result by sending that owned value onward, again by move, not by shared mutation.

Atomics where a counter or flag is enough: update metrics and the shutdown flag. A request counter or error counter is one word, so an AtomicU64 with fetch_add(1, Relaxed) suffices and needs no lock; a relaxed ordering is fine because counters need no happens-before relationship with other state. A graceful-shutdown flag is an AtomicBool, published with Release and observed with Acquire if it gates other state.

For production measurement before upgrading to a more complex primitive: instrument lock wait time and lock hold time on any Mutex or RwLock, queue depth and enqueue latency on the channels, condvar wakeup rate if a condvar is used, and end-to-end retry latency. Upgrade only when those numbers show a real bottleneck, and keep lock-free structures off the critical path until a measured requirement appears, because they imply unsafe code and a memory-reclamation story that is rarely worth it. One service legitimately uses several primitives at once: Arc snapshots for routing and config, atomics for metrics, a Mutex only for the contended retry table, and channels for the work queue and result handoff. The cleanest version keeps each mutable subsystem under one owner.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One service, several primitives: Arc snapshots for routing/config, an atomic counter for metrics, and bounded channels for the work queue and result handoff.
criteria: At least one subsystem is assigned to channels (work queue and result handoff) and at least one to shared state or atomics (metrics counter, retry table), each with a reason.
The RwLock/config choice is justified by a read-mostly access pattern, and the immutable Arc-swap alternative is offered when the config is replaced wholesale.
At least one observability hook is named (lock wait time, queue depth, condvar wakeup rate, or retry latency) as the trigger for any upgrade.
Lock-free structures are kept off the critical path until a measured requirement appears.

labSolution.explanation:
The lab implements the canonical release/acquire publication pattern. publish first stores the payload 42 with Ordering::Relaxed, then stores true into the ready flag with Ordering::Release. The Release store is the publication edge: it guarantees that the preceding relaxed write to value is visible to any thread that later performs an Acquire load which observes the flag as true.

try_consume does the matching half. It loads ready with Ordering::Acquire, and only if that load observes true does it load the payload. The Acquire load pairs with the writer's Release store to establish a happens-before relationship, so the relaxed load of value is guaranteed to see 42 rather than the initial 0. The payload itself stays relaxed deliberately: the flag, not the payload load, carries the ordering edge, which is the whole point the chapter draws out in the atomics-and-ordering section.

In this single-threaded main the writes obviously complete before the reads, so the ordering choice does not change the printed result here; the program prints ready = true then value = 42. The Release/Acquire pairing is what makes the same code correct when publish and try_consume run on different threads, which is the design the chapter's Example 3 demonstrates with thread::scope. The fix over the starter code is precisely upgrading the flag store to Release and the flag loads to Acquire while leaving the payload relaxed.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is `RwLock` not automatically better than `Mutex`?
reviewAnswers.answer: An RwLock is a different fairness and contention trade, not a faster mutex. It lets multiple readers hold the lock at once, but a writer must wait for every reader to leave and then excludes everyone, so under frequent writes the writer can stall or starve and throughput can fall below a plain mutex. It also does more bookkeeping to track reader counts, which can cost more than the contention it removes when each critical section is tiny. RwLock pays off only when access is genuinely read-mostly with non-trivial read sections; otherwise a Mutex is calmer and often faster.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should a condvar wait happen in a loop instead of a one-shot `if`?
reviewAnswers.answer: Because a condvar wakeup does not promise the predicate is now true; it only signals that the waiter should re-check. Spurious wakeups are permitted, a notify_all can wake several waiters when only one item arrived, and another thread may consume the state before the woken thread re-acquires the lock. A while loop re-evaluates the mutex-protected predicate after every wakeup and only exits when the predicate genuinely holds, whereas an if would let the thread proceed on a false wakeup and act on state that is not actually ready. The mutex-protected predicate, not the condvar, is the source of truth.

reviewAnswers.question: What does `Release` on a store and `Acquire` on a load actually buy you?
reviewAnswers.answer: Together they create a happens-before edge between two threads through one shared atomic. A Release store guarantees that all writes the writer performed before it become visible to any thread whose Acquire load later observes that store, so the Acquire reader is guaranteed to see everything the writer did beforehand. This is what lets a single flag publish other data: the writer releases the flag, the reader acquires it, and the reader can then trust the relaxed payload writes that preceded the release. Without that pairing the reader has no ordering guarantee and may observe stale values on a weakly ordered machine.

reviewAnswers.question: When is a barrier the right tool, and when is it just the wrong primitive for state propagation?
reviewAnswers.answer: A barrier is the right tool for a phase boundary: it makes n threads all reach a point before any of them proceeds, which is exactly what you want for a startup start-gun or for separating distinct computation phases. It is a synchronization gate, not a data container, and it holds no state of its own. It is the wrong primitive when you actually need to propagate or share a value, because the barrier conveys only the fact that everyone arrived, not any data; for that you still need a lock, an atomic publication, an immutable snapshot, or a channel. Reaching for a barrier to move state confuses 'everyone is here now' with 'everyone can see the new value.'

reviewAnswers.question: Why are lock-free structures hard even for experienced engineers?
reviewAnswers.answer: Lock-free structures replace the simple mutual-exclusion contract of a lock with explicit memory ordering, which means reasoning directly about Acquire, Release, and the visibility of every write across threads on weakly ordered hardware. In real implementations they almost always require unsafe code plus a memory reclamation strategy, since you cannot free a node while another thread might still be reading it, leading to hazard pointers, epoch-based reclamation, or similar machinery. Subtle bugs like the ABA problem and rare orderings that only surface under specific timing make them hard to test and hard to prove correct. That is why 'avoid all locks' is not a mature design principle on its own, and lock-free structures belong off the critical path until a measured requirement justifies the cost.
